newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-Soviet dissident returns to jail to test change.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet dissident returns to jail to test change.

text.p: Israeli minister Natan Sharansky returned on Thursday to the former KGB prison where he spent some of his darkest days as a Soviet dissident to test how far Russia had changed since he left.

"I'm going back to my alma mater, it was the most important university I studied at in my life," Sharansky told a horde of reporters, kept back from the notorious jail by masked elite troops armed with truncheons.
After almost an hour and a half, Sharansky emerged from the Lefortovo prison where, a decade earlier, he had spent a year and a half in isolation, threatened with execution for treason.
He shook hands with prison officials before giving a mixed verdict on the prison, now used by the Federal Security Service -- the post-communist KGB -- for suspects awaiting trial.
"It's very clean, much cleaner, and was looking nice. I thank the prison administration for making such a big effort," said Sharansky, who is now Israel's trade and industry minister.

"It is the same prison with the same cells where there is absolute silence, where not a single sound is permitted, with the same, very tough punishment cell. I can say, I was in many punishment cells and Lefortovo prison had by far the worst."

He said he had not expected officials to apologise for the way he was treated during his time at Lefortovo or in the prison camp where he spent nine years before being handed over to the West in a dramatic prisoner exchange.
Sharansky, then known as Anatoly Shcharansky, was refused permission to leave in Soviet Union in 1973 on what he was told were security grounds.
He became a leading campaigner for Jewish emigration rights and in 1977 was charged with being an agent of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency.
"I was a man fighting against the people, the system so it wasn't a question of an apology," Sharansky said.

"It was a question of returning to the past and trying to understand through Lefortovo prison how big the changes in the country have been because I think one can tell a lot about society through a prison and one cannot deceive me with it."

Sharansky said the prisoners were given more meat than in his day, that radios and light had appeared in the cells and that he was told that in the punishment cell they got blankets at night and the same food as the other prisoners.
"That would be a big improvement if it is true," he said, betraying a hint of scepticism.
The biggest loss, he said, was the prison library, now filled with detective novels.

"It was the biggest library I have seen in Russia which contained priceless classical tomes confiscated from people in the 1930s. It gave me a lot of strength in the most difficult periods of interrogation," he said.
Sharansky said he was initially told that the punishment cell where he had been was no longer used, but was later shown it. "It clearly was being used," he said.

Summing up, he said he thought not all was as it seemed. "On the face of it there were a whole series of changes," he said. "I saw a prisoner in a punishment cell but I didn't talk to him because I had the feeling that all this had been staged."
Sharansky saw more dramatic changes when he went to a school where orthodox Jewish children were learning about their religious traditions and hearing about past discrimination under communism.
The visit wound up a four-day trip, during which Sharansky met officials to try to improve trade between Israel and Russia and revisited friends who had fought with him for human rights.
